title: Negative Slope: What It Really Means

scenes.title: Why is this slope negative?
body: Look at the line through (-1, 4), (0, 2), and (1, 0).
A negative slope means y decreases as x increases.
scenes.narration: Suppose a line passes through negative one four, zero two, and one zero. Here is the idea: slope tells you the direction and rate of change. When x moves to the right, y is going down. That downward direction is exactly what makes the slope negative.

scenes.title: Read the movement, not just the sign
scenes.narration: From zero two to one zero, x increases by one, while y decreases by two. So the rise is negative two and the run is positive one. Negative two divided by one gives a slope of negative two. Notice why the minus sign is there: it records the downward change in y.

scenes.title: This is where students mix things up
body: Negative slope does NOT mean the y-intercept is negative.
It describes direction, not where the line crosses the y-axis.
scenes.narration: This is where students often mix things up. A negative slope does not mean the y-intercept must be negative. In y equals m x plus b, m controls the direction of the line. Here m is negative two, but b is positive two. Those are two different jobs.

scenes.title: Why the equation matches the graph
body: m = -2 means down 2 for every right 1.
b = 2 means the line crosses the y-axis at (0, 2).
scenes.narration: The equation y equals negative two x plus two tells the whole story. The negative two says that every one-unit increase in x produces a two-unit decrease in y. The plus two says the line starts at y equals two when x equals zero. That is why the graph falls from left to right and still crosses the y-axis above zero.

scenes.title: Quick check
body: The point (1, 0) is on the line.
scenes.narration: Quick check: substitute x equals one. Negative two times one plus two equals zero, so the point one zero fits the equation. The main idea is simple: a negative slope means the output decreases as the input increases. Do not confuse that with the sign of the intercept. The full lesson is available on SUMMIT.
